hero.headline: The control premium
hero.subtitle: For years, retail rewarded those who moved fastest. Now it favours those who understand what they actually own.

sections.content: cross the NORA ecosystem, a recalibration is underway — subtle in tone, but significant in consequence. Growth has not disappeared as an ambition, but it is no longer the organising principle. Control is.
This shift is not ideological. It is being forced.

Customer acquisition costs have hardened. Demand signals are less predictable. And the infrastructure underpinning modern retail — from marketplaces to fulfilment networks — has become increasingly externalised. What once felt like leverage is now being re-examined as dependency.

In response, a new discipline is emerging inside executive teams — one that asks harder, more structural questions: Where does value actually accrue? Who owns the customer relationship? And what, if anything, is defensible?
The Three Patterns

First, data is being redefined as a control asset, not a by-product. The conversation has moved beyond collection toward cohesion. Without a unified view of the customer, the promise of AI, personalisation and retail media remains largely theoretical.
Second, operational simplicity is being treated as a strategic lever. Complexity, long masked as sophistication, is being unwound. The advantage is shifting toward those who can operate with clarity.
Third, margin is reclaiming its position as a design constraint. Not an outcome, but an input. Growth that cannot sustain margin is increasingly viewed as erosion in disguise.
Individually, these moves are pragmatic. Collectively, they signal a transition from expansion-led retail to structurally disciplined retail.
From the Boardroom
What makes this shift notable is not the theory, but how consistently it is echoed by senior leaders navigating it in real time.
“We scaled faster than we understood our own business. Now we’re going back to rebuild the spine — data, systems, ownership. Growth exposed the gaps.”
“Everyone talks about AI, but most organisations don’t have decision-ready data. The issue isn’t intelligence — it’s coherence.”
“We used to treat margin as something we’d fix later. Now it’s the first filter.”
“We’ve outsourced more of the customer journey than we realised. The question now is — what’s left that’s uniquely ours?”

Some describe this as the emergence of the agentic retailer — where decision-making is faster, systems more autonomous, and leadership less about orchestration. But beneath the language sits a simpler truth: in a system increasingly shaped by platforms, partners and intelligent machines, control is becoming the premium. And those who cannot clearly define it are unlikely to capture it.

article2.title: An analogue lens in a digital AI world

hero.headline: An analogue lens in a digital AI world
hero.subtitle:
"Technology challenges us to assert our human values, which means that first of all, we have to figure out what they are."
— Sherry Turkle
hero.byline: By featured writer: Paul Greenberg, chair, NORA

sections.content: was at a high-tech show in Las Vegas a few years ago. The latest high-resolution technology was on dazzling display. Keynote speakers spoke passionately about the chip revolution and the promise of artificial intelligence.

I should have been immersing myself completely in the innovation and the latest insights. I had been a regular attendee at these techfests for decades. Yet, for the first time, I found myself strangely disconnected from the buzz. Walking past a merchandise stand, I spotted a black T-shirt with the words “An Analogue Soul Caught in a Digital World” printed across the front.
I smiled and bought the shirt.

I entered the world of ecommerce as a digital immigrant in the mid-1990s, gathering momentum through the late '90s and the 2000s. Today, I still work in and around technology-led commerce—primarily as an investor, adviser and board member. Keeping pace with the relentless speed of technological change is becoming increasingly difficult. Is that simply a function of age? I don't think so.

Rather, I have consciously chosen to occupy a respectful contrarian position to the dominant narrative of a future driven almost entirely by technology—one where AI is said to be "eating the world." As is often the case, these predictions are highly binary and tend to overlook the lessons I've learnt over the past three decades.
The biggest lesson?

The game is almost always played—and won—down the middle of the field. Around 2014 or 2015, I was credited with coining the term phygital. In truth, I doubt I deserve the credit; I probably first heard it at one of the retail conferences in the US or Europe. But the truth behind the term resonated deeply with me then, and it still does today.

In a nutshell, phygital captured the idea that the best retailers would embrace both the physical and digital pathways to the customer. At a time when pure-play ecommerce was rapidly gaining traction, I, along with many industry peers, came to the conclusion that customers shop by brand, not by channel.

As an industry, we were in danger of developing what I called "channel fever" — an obsession with choosing a lane when our customers never did. They moved effortlessly between physical stores, websites and mobile devices, expecting us to do the same.
Eventually, we learnt. We adapted. Today, what was once called multi-channel retail has become simply… retail.
I sense that commerce is once again approaching one of these binary crossroads.
This time, the choice appears to be between artificial intelligence and human connection. I suspect that, once again, the winning strategy will lie somewhere in between.

The intersection between this extraordinary AI technology and a deeper understanding of customers will require as much traditional analogue thinking as it will a wholehearted embrace of AI tools. Success will come not from choosing one over the other, but from integrating both.
However, while the strategy may be non-binary, our professional expertise may not be.

As practitioners, I suspect we will increasingly need to choose where we develop true mastery. The depth of knowledge required to remain at the forefront of AI is immense. Equally, developing deep expertise in consumer psychology, anthropology, behavioural science and human motivation is a lifelong pursuit. It will become progressively harder to be world-class in both.
I've made my choice.
I'm doubling down on the human side of the commerce equation.
I proudly declare myself an analogue proponent.

That doesn’t mean becoming a technological Luddite. Far from it. I'll remain curious and continue experimenting with the remarkable technologies emerging around us and the countless opportunities they present.

But I make no apology for returning to my roots as a student of the humanities. I began my career in psychological services as a young organisational psychologist. It is with that lens that I increasingly see my career reaching its natural conclusion. In many ways, I've come full circle.
If a young person asked me today what they should study, my advice would be surprisingly simple. Study one of two things exceptionally well.

Either become deeply technical—immersing yourself in AI, machine learning and advanced computing—or immerse yourself in the humanities: psychology, sociology, anthropology, philosophy, history and ethics.
The future will belong to those who can either build intelligent machines or deeply understand the humans who use them.

In fact, I suspect the much-maligned Bachelor of Arts is quietly making a comeback. As AI commoditises technical capability, uniquely human capabilities—curiosity, judgement, empathy, creativity and wisdom—become more valuable, not less.
The new world won't be built by technology alone.
It will be built at the intersection of science and humanity.
Perhaps that T-shirt from Las Vegas was less a joke than a prediction. I'm proudly an analogue soul, happily living—and working—in a digital world.”

I will leave the final word to Steve Jobs, whose philosophy perhaps captured this balance better than anyone: "Technology is nothing. What's important is that you have faith in people, that they rebasically good and smart, and if you give them tools, they'll do wonderful things with them."

article3.title: National advantage: why Australia’s retail future won’t be built on cost

hero.headline: National advantage: why Australia’s retail future won’t be built on cost
hero.subtitle: For decades, Australian retail has been fighting a battle it can never truly win: cost. Competing on price alone is a race to the bottom, but thriving retailers are focusing on relevance.

sections.content: or decades, Australian retail has been fighting a battle it can never truly win: cost. Against global marketplaces, endless supply chains and international scale, competing on price alone is a race to the bottom. Yet many of the retailers thriving today have stopped asking how to be cheaper and started asking how to be more relevant.
National advantage in the next decade won’t come from lower labour costs or larger warehouses. It will come from trust, proximity, agility and community.

Australian retailers understand Australian customers better than anyone. They know local seasons, local values, local culture and local expectations. In an age where AI makes products infinitely discoverable and marketplaces make everything available, differentiation shifts from product access to customer intimacy.
The winners won’t be the biggest retailers. They’ll be the retailers that turn local insight into strategic advantage.
Perhaps the real question isn’t how Australia competes with the world.
It’s how the world competes with retailers who genuinely understand Australia.

article4.title: What AI in retail needs from the systems underneath it

hero.headline: What AI in retail needs from the systems underneath it
hero.subtitle: Australian retailers are investing heavily in AI. Far fewer have a record their systems can safely act on. A look at why this difference decides which retailers get useful work out of agents and which find agents acting on numbers that were already wrong.

sections.content: he Australian retail sector has settled the question of whether to invest in AI, with 83.4% of retailers expecting AI and agentic commerce to change how shoppers buy. Investment is already directed at product content, onsite search, personalisation and customer service.
The problem is no longer access to AI models. What retailers lack is a record those models can be trusted to read.
Why agentic AI changes the data problem
Generative AI tolerates imperfect data. When the output is a product description or drafted customer email, a person reviews it before anyone else does.

Agentic work is different. Someone approving a replenishment order sees the quantity the agent has proposed, but not necessarily the stock position it read to get there. If that position came from systems that had not reconciled, the quantity can look reasonable and still be wrong. The error is in the input rather than the output, making it much harder to catch.

Research shows the sector splitting along that line. 66% of retail respondents are using generative models and large language models, against 58% elsewhere. On agentic AI in production, the ordering reverses: 29% for retail against 32% across industries.
Retail is ahead on the technology that produces drafts and behind on the technology that produces actions.

The most instructive demonstration came from OpenAI. Instant Checkout, which let shoppers buy inside ChatGPT, launched in September 2025 and was withdrawn in March 2026, with Forrester attributing the retreat in part to product data that was frequently wrong on stock availability, delivery timing and shipping cost.
Even access to leading AI models could not overcome unreliable underlying product data.
What does an agent need to act?
An agent needs current data, consistent definitions, clear permissions and an audit trail.

This is where the underlying ERP becomes critical. But having an ERP is not the same as having consolidated onto one. If warehouse, inventory, order and finance systems still hold different versions of the truth, the reconciliation problem remains.
For retailers that have consolidated properly, the opportunities are fairly immediate.
Where agents can start doing the work

Replenishment is often the first candidate. An agent can watch what is selling, check stock on hand and what’s already on order, then propose a quantity for approval. But it only works if there is one reliable inventory number to read.

Order exceptions are another opportunity. If an item isn’t available at the warehouse due to ship it, an agent can determine whether to split the shipment, source it elsewhere or issue a refund. But that decision depends on live stock and order data sitting together.

Supplier invoice matching is even more mechanical. An agent can compare the invoice, purchase order and goods receipt, passing clean matches through to payment and escalating discrepancies. Where those records sit in separate systems, the reconciliation problem remains.
Governance can’t come afterwards

Governance is where the sequencing usually goes wrong. Oxford Economics found that 49% of businesses report AI agents have already taken incorrect actions during pilots or deployment, while 43% have no human-in-the-loop process for agentic workflows at all.

An ERP arrives with many of those controls already in place, including role-based permissions, approval thresholds, delegation rules and audit logging. A control enforced by the system can be demonstrated to an auditor. An instruction sitting in an agent’s prompt cannot.
The foundation is the strategy
Most retailers still rate their data foundations as some way short of ready, with identity resolution and single customer view among the capabilities furthest behind.

But that gap also describes how few competitors have done the work, which is what makes doing it valuable. A retailer with one reliable record can put agents into replenishment and exception handling and take cost out of both. A retailer without one is buying tools that sit on top of the same reconciliation problem and paying people to bridge it.
Retail’s AI constraint has moved somewhere less exciting than the discussion suggests. The differentiator is not the model or the tooling, both of which are available to everyone on comparable terms.
It is whether the systems underneath can hand work to each other without a person in the middle translating between them.
The foundation is not what a retailer builds before the strategy. It is the strategy.

article5.title: Powerful partnerships: the end of the hero retailer

hero.headline:
Powerful partnerships:
The end of the hero retailer
hero.subtitle: A new era of super compliance is fast approaching.

sections.content: etail has long celebrated the myth of the hero retailer—the organisation that succeeds through its own brilliance, innovation and execution.
That era is ending.

The most significant breakthroughs in retail today are increasingly occurring between organisations, not within them. Retailers partnering with technology companies. Competitors collaborating on sustainability. Brands sharing data. Industry networks solving common challenges together.
The complexity facing retail has become too great for any single organisation to solve alone.
Yet many businesses still approach partnerships transactionally: procurement-led, short-term and focused on immediate outcomes.
The strongest partnerships are different. They create shared intelligence, shared opportunity and shared advantage.
The question for leaders is no longer, “Who are our competitors?”
It’s becoming, “Who are our collaborators?”
In a connected economy, the future belongs to ecosystems, not empires.

article6.title: Next Gen purpose: why younger consumers are redefining success

hero.headline: Next Gen purpose: why younger consumers are redefining success
hero.subtitle: For years, purpose was treated as a marketing exercise. A campaign. A statement. A sustainability report.

sections.content: he next generation sees it differently. For younger consumers and employees, purpose isn’t what a company says. It’s what a company does when nobody is looking.

They are increasingly questioning business models built on endless consumption, disposable products and short-term thinking. They expect transparency, accountability and impact—not because it’s fashionable, but because they see these issues as fundamental to the future they will inherit.
This creates an uncomfortable challenge for retail.
Can an industry historically designed to drive more consumption evolve into one that creates more value with less waste?
The organisations that answer this question convincingly will attract customers, talent and trust.
The ones that don’t may discover that purpose is no longer optional.
It’s becoming a licence to operate.

article8.title: Behind the scenes at THE ICONIC

hero.headline: Behind the scenes at THE ICONIC
hero.subtitle: In late October, NORA took around 30 retailers through THE ICONIC’s Yennora fulfilment centre. Here’s what we saw on the floor, and why the way the tour was run made it different.

sections.content: Under the hood at THE ICONIC

n July, at our first Operations Leaders Velocity Summit, our industry hosts Mick Bunt and Kieran Boyce put a simple question to around 120 Ops leaders in the room. If you could get under the hood of one retailer and see how they fulfil, who would it be?
The answer was overwhelming, in the room and again in the survey afterwards: THE ICONIC.
It’s not hard to see why. THE ICONIC keeps raising the bar on delivery, most recently with DoorDash delivery for customers in metro Sydney, and early signs are strong.
In late October, we took a group of retailers through their Yennora fulfilment centre.
The best ideas for this series come from the people in it. Ops leaders want to see how others work at scale, and a few hours on someone else’s floor often answers questions a summit session can’t.
A tour where no one was stuck at the back

You can invest in the best technology in the world, but it's the people who ultimately make an operation successful. What Sue and her team have built at THE ICONIC is a great example of that. You could see the investment in their people, the ownership across the warehouse and the genuine commitment to continuous improvement. That's what makes an operation like this so impressive.
sections.attribution: Mon Larsen, Head of Sales & Partnerships at Starshipit

sections.content: We’ve run some great tours this year, at Shiperoo, The Winning Group and Culture Kings. This one was different, and the difference was in how Sue Wood, THE ICONIC’s Director of Operations, set it up.

Around 30 retailers joined us, from pure play ecommerce to store-based businesses. Rather than one big group shuffling between stations, Sue brought her team in to lead groups of four or five. Each tour ran for about an hour and a half.
No one was stuck at the back. Everyone could see, and everyone could ask the questions they actually came with.

That format tells you a lot about a leadership team. Sue trusted her people to walk other retailers through their own operation and share what they know. The knowledge doesn’t sit with one or two people at COO or director level. It’s spread across the team, and they’re proud to share it.
What you could see on the floor
I was in Sue’s group. Sue knew the names of everyone on the floor, and there were a lot of them. Whatever we asked, she had the answer.

The site was busy but calm. People knew what they were working on, where the operation is at and where it’s heading. You could see how the teams are run and how they’re incentivised, and it showed in the work.

Mick summed it up well afterwards. You can read a culture by how the floor reacts when senior leaders walk through. Do people scramble to look busy, or keep doing their job and say g’day? At THE ICONIC it was the latter. Sue runs the operation in a clear order: safety, service, then cost. People first, and the results follow.
A sense check before peak
After the tour, THE ICONIC looked after us with morning tea and we sat down together for an open, peer-led conversation. Mick and Kieran did a great job driving the conversation.

Retailers brought their real challenges: managing teams through volume, incentives, returns, what’s working and what isn’t. Sue and her team answered everything openly, including what they’re still working on.

With peak season about to hit, the timing was right. It was a chance to sense check plans against a business that handles serious fulfillment volume every day, and to hear from peers facing the same pressure.
Thank you
THE ICONIC has supported NORA across many of our events, and plenty of their leaders were in the room at the Velocity Summit. It was a pleasure to take that relationship onto their floor.
Thank you to Rostin and Sue and to all of the team, who were brilliant. They gave us half a day, a lot of honest answers and a genuinely warm welcome.
Thank you to Mick and Kieran for their ongoing commitment to this community, and to our series partner Starshipit and supporting partner Descartes, who make programs like this possible.
And thank you to every retailer who turned up, asked questions and gave their time. That’s what makes this community work.
Where should we go next? We’d love to hear from you: gareth@nora.org.au

hero.headline: The complexity economy
hero.subtitle: The retailers quietly building competitive advantage with Feedonomics

sections.content: or much of the past two decades, retail strategy has been relatively straightforward: reach more customers, through more channels, with greater convenience. And to a large extent this has worked for many of us.

Marketplaces opened new audiences. Social commerce shortened the path to purchase. Click & collect reshaped fulfilment. Retail media created new revenue streams. International expansion became more accessible than ever.
The industry became exceptionally good at creating new opportunities.
Less attention was paid to what those opportunities demanded in return.

Every additional channel brought another set of merchandising rules. Another catalogue to maintain. Another taxonomy. Another image specification. Another pricing structure. None of these requirements were particularly difficult on their own. Together, they have created an operating environment that looks fundamentally different from the one retailers were designed to manage.
This is one of the more interesting shifts occurring in retail.

The conversation around productivity still tends to focus on labour, supply chains and automation. Yet one of the fastest-growing sources of operational cost is complexity itself ...not complexity imposed by regulation or macroeconomic conditions, but complexity created as businesses pursue growth.
The irony is that many of retail's best strategic decisions have also become its greatest operational challenge.

Selling through more channels is sensible. Expanding product ranges is sensible. Localising assortments is again sensible. The question is no longer whether retailers should pursue these opportunities, but how they prevent each one from introducing another layer of operational friction.

As retailers prepare for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, the cost of complexity becomes harder to ignore. Peak trading doesn't create operational weaknesses; it exposes them. The systems and processes that support product data across every channel are suddenly placed under greater pressure, making preparation as much about operational readiness as inventory and fulfilment.

This is why disciplines that once sat quietly inside ecommerce teams are moving into the centre of retail operations. Product information management is one example. What was once regarded as administrative work has become part of the infrastructure required to support modern commerce. As retailers such as APG & Co. and City Beach have demonstrated in their partnership with Feedonomics - improving the consistency and governance of product information doesn't simply tidy up data, it reduces manual effort, improves channel performance and allows organisations to scale without proportionally increasing operational overhead. Feedonomics customers report spending up to 43% less time managing product feeds, illustrating how simplifying complexity can create operational capacity rather than simply reducing effort.
The invitation for retailers is to consider the complexity of their product information and to seize the opportunities to alleviate this with intelligence.

Retail's competitive advantage is becoming less about adding complexity than mastering it. As an industry we must discern how we are contributing to our internal complexity economy and be open to transformative ways to simplify.

article10.title: The next generation of POS: What Australian retailers need from their technology partner

hero.headline: The next generation of POS: What Australian retailers need from their technology partner
hero.subtitle: Why the right solution partner matters as much as the platform

sections.content: In this episode of The NORA Edit, we sit down with Tim Sheedy, Founder and Principal Analyst at Singularity Research, and Mahesh Krishnan, Chief Technology Officer at Fujitsu Oceania, to discuss how Australian retailers can modernise their point of sale systems without risking downtime or peak trading disruptions. Discover what separates successful rollouts from costly mistakes and learn the critical questions to ask before selecting your tech partner.
Podcast overview

sections.title: The Next Generation of POS – Fujitsu podcast

sections.content: Is your legacy point of sale system quietly eating into your margins? Between workarounds on the shop floor, inflexible promotions and online returns clogging up the counter, the hidden costs of holding onto an outdated system add up fast.

In this session, Tim and Mahesh break down how to time your upgrade right and roll out across your store network without losing a day of trading. Drawing on decades of industry experience and some of the world’s largest POS deployments, they cut through the tech jargon and focus on what matters to retailers.

We’ll explore why choosing the right delivery partner is just as critical as the software platform itself. The real test is evidence, and the best evidence comes from peers. Tim’s recent research into how Australian technology leaders buy found that peer recommendation is still the number one reason one solution partner is chosen over another. He shares how to vet solution partners by talking directly to retailers who have deployed the exact same software at scale, and the one question that tells you most: how did your partner respond when something went wrong?

Mahesh then draws on his experience as a CTO and his global perspective on large-scale POS rollouts. He shares what separates the programs that land smoothly from those that struggle, and the practical steps that keep stores trading while the change happens.

The conversation also takes a grounded look at the next three to five years. Moving past the AI hype, the focus is on connected stores where checkout, cash handling and loss prevention work as one, simpler integrations in place of years of layered omnichannel builds, and a platform that can keep adapting without ripping out the core.
Both guests agree on the first step, and it isn’t a technology purchase. Listen to the end to hear why clean data, and a shopper reading an ingredients list, sit at the heart of what comes next.

Whether a point of sale overhaul is on your roadmap or you are just starting to explore your options, this conversation provides guidance on what to ask, what to test and what good looks like on the shop floor.

hero.headline: Velocity summit 2026 wrap-up
hero.subtitle: More than 120 operations, supply chain, fulfilment and last-mile leaders gathered for the first operations leaders’ velocity summit. Kieran Boyce shares what stuck with him, and why honest conversations about what went wrong are worth more than the highlight reel.
hero.byline: By Kieran Boyce, Retail Fulfillment & Digital Operations Lead, MECCA

sections.content: What LinkedIn doesn’t show you

croll this platform on any given day and you’ll see all of our best days. Promotions, keynotes, panel wins, the photo with the good lighting. LinkedIn is our highlight reel. What you won’t see much of: the almighty screw-up, the delivery promise that failed a customer, the 2am anxiety-ridden replay in your head of the meeting that didn’t go to plan.

Operations is at the front-line of most businesses, that means they’re deep in the chaos ruthlessly prioritising in real time. The brutal fact is we don’t always get it right. You’d be hard pressed to find someone writing a long post, with all the beautiful emojis and tags about the day they got it wrong.

Authenticity and vulnerability in operations leadership come from exactly those moments, the ones we don’t post about. We call it experience once we’ve survived it; it’s what you get immediately after you needed it... That’s the premise the Velocity stream was built on over the past 12 months: build a forum where that experience gets shared honestly, instead of curated into another highlight reel. Don’t pull up the ladder behind us as leaders. Set the stage for the future leaders and operators by giving them something useful.

At Velocity 2026 that premise got a proper run. More than 120 retail operations, supply chain, fulfilment and last-mile leaders filled a room at The Grounds of Alexandria for the first Operations Leaders’ Velocity Summit, run by the NORA ~ National Online Retailers Association. Mick Bunt and I joined forces to host. It was the culmination of a year of warehouse tours, roundtables and conversations with the people keeping retail moving, including visits behind the scenes at Shiperoo, Winning Group and Culture Kings. Those tours shaped a lot of what made it into the room on the day.
Here’s what stuck with me.
Efficiency is dead, intelligence wins

I sat on a panel with Toni Baston Woolworths MarketPlus (Gee I miss working with you Toni, when Mick & I discussed the speaker list you were one of the first names that came up as authenticity personified!) and Shane Alexander (King Living), hosted by Mick (3PO), under the banner of “Efficiency is Dead. Intelligence Wins.”

sections.alt: Kieran, Toni, Shane and Mick seated on stools on stage during the panel
sections.caption: Kieran, Toni, Shane & Mick (Left to Right).

sections.content: Shane made a point that’s stayed with me. When you’re delivering high-end furniture, shaving two minutes off a delivery window is the wrong metric. His drivers need more time in the home, not less. Customer delight and margin protection in heavy goods come from intelligence applied to the last mile, not from stopwatch thinking. Experience matters.

I put a version of that same tension to the room from a experiential retail angle. Traditional supply chain thinking wants to standardise everything it touches. Standardisation of service eventually reaches a point where it strips out the touch customers are actually paying for (and expect). The job is finding that point and using data to protect it without blowing out cost.
The bigger point underneath all of it: digital and supply chain used to sit in separate silos. They don’t anymore, and any leader still running them that way is maintaining a obsolete structure.
Operations doesn’t stop at the warehouse door

Hakan Steele from Starshipit hosted a panel with three operators who’ve each scaled fast and have the scars to show for it: Joel Randal (Culture Kings), Jodie Tarasek (MESHKI) and Ty Cooper (Muscle Republic).

Ty’s point on headcount resonated most with anyone who’s operated a warehouse through a peak. Doubling your warehouse headcount doesn’t double your productivity. Without clear process, experienced leads and structured onboarding, more people just create more bottlenecks. Joel’s contribution was about where operational risk actually sits: not always inside the warehouse, but in the gap between marketing, ops, CX and tech when a campaign launches before all four have planned it together. Get that wrong and you’re looking at oversold inventory and a customer experience that takes weeks to recover - and potentially thousands of customers who will never shop with you again.

Jodie’s framing was great: Customers don’t separate your marketing, your warehouse, your customer service or your carriers. They remember whether the experience they were promised got delivered. Abi Bennett from Starshipit put it plainly in a note she sent after the session:
Operations is no longer simply supporting the brand experience. Increasingly, it is the brand experience.
sections.attribution: Abi Bennett, Starshipit

sections.content: She left the room asking two questions worth sitting with. (1) Could your next campaign overwhelm your operation? and; (2) Are you measuring what customers actually notice, rather than what your internal efficiency reports say?

sections.alt: Hakan, Ty, Jodie and Joel on stage in front of a screen showing their names
sections.caption: Hakan, Ty, Jodie & Joel (Left to Right)

sections.content: The end of business as usual

Guy Nappa, COO of Oz Hair and Beauty, sat down with Mick for a fireside on what he called the end of business as usual. Guy’s business has been on a fierce growth curve for years. The conversation covered what breaks under that kind of growth: the role he used to do versus the role he does now, priorities that shift every six months whether you’re ready or not, and the mindset required to keep making decisive calls without waiting for things to settle.
The advice that stuck: navigating rapid growth means constantly deciding what to stop doing. There’s never going to be more time to find.
Diversity of decisions, not diversity of headcount

Mina Shi (LIONESS) closed out the afternoon on diversity in supply chain, and the framing was sharper than the topic usually gets. Their point: diversity of background and perspective is what produces better decisions, better teams and better businesses. That’s the measure worth tracking.

It’s a common thematic that operations leaders often tread their path unconventially. The “10-years-on-the-floor” is the exception pathway for modern leaders. This was it’s own useful reminder that the pipeline for operations talent is wider than the industry usually treats it, and diversity of thought can be unlocked by embracing it.

What I also took in this session was leadership from the back of the room. Brian Nguyen showing strong support. This is one of those unsung moments where a C-Suite executive take the time to support one of their team. It’s meaningful. People remember how you make them feel.

sections.alt: Abi and Mina on stage in front of large arched windows
sections.caption: Abi & Mina (Left to Right)

sections.content: Where to next?

We built this stream because the tours, roundtables and now the summit kept surfacing the same thing: the operators willing to talk honestly about what went wrong learn faster than the ones only willing to talk about what went right. That’s an uncomfortable thing to build a public forum around, but it’s the version we believe is worth building.

The next generation of operations leaders is watching how the current one talks about failure. If all we show them is the highlight reel, we’re teaching them to hide the parts of the job that actually build judgement, experience and ultimately - value.
So here’s the question I’m sitting with after the day: if you stripped the highlight reel out of your own LinkedIn history, what would be left?

article12.title: Can AI make recruitment more human? Wingstop Australia thinks so.

hero.headline: Can AI make recruitment more human? Wingstop Australia thinks so.
hero.subtitle: As retailers turn to AI to tackle recruitment pressures, Wingstop Australia is showing how automation can speed up hiring without losing the personal nuance.
hero.byline: With Fleur Brennet, Workday and Jono Spragg, Wingstop Australia
hero.videoAlt: Staff working in a quick-service restaurant kitchen behind a stainless-steel counter

sections.content: reater recruitment efficiency presents a dilemma. For candidates, automated recruitment can feel impersonal, reducing what should be a human interaction to a series of questions, automated responses and algorithmic decisions.
The challenge for retailers is not simply how much of the hiring process they can automate, but also how to make the experience better for the people going through it.

It’s a question becoming more pressing as the industry faces growing recruitment demands. Retail trade vacancies rose 24.5 per cent in the three months to August 2026, the largest percentage increase of any industry, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
For Wingstop Australia, which opened its first store in 2025 and now has six, with plans for 110, the challenge was particularly acute.

Each new store requires between 40 and 80 crew members. With a new opening planned approximately every six weeks, the business needed a recruitment process that could keep pace with its expansion without overwhelming store managers or alienating potential employees.

Jono Spragg, Wingstop Australia’s Director of Operations, was initially sceptical about using AI in recruitment. Eighteen months ago, he says, he would have “switched off” at the suggestion of a bot managing the hiring conversation.
But years working in hospitality had also shown him how inefficient traditional recruitment could be.
Managers would post advertisements, work through hundreds of résumés and often rely on personal familiarity when deciding whom to interview. Arranging a single interview could take two weeks.
At Wingstop’s planned rate of expansion, that approach would quickly become a bottleneck.
Enter Ranchy
The business turned to Workday Paradox, a conversational AI recruitment assistant, implementing the technology before its first Australian store opened.

Rather than deploying a generic recruitment bot, Wingstop customised the experience around its own brand, creating “Ranchy”, a talking tub of ranch dressing that guides applicants through the hiring process.
The company deliberately made it clear that candidates were interacting with a bot, while tailoring its language to feel conversational and approachable.
Spragg established a guiding principle: make the initial conversation “as automated as possible”, with “human feeling language on top of it”.
The approach was not about removing people from recruitment. It was about removing the repetitive administrative tasks that prevented managers from spending time with candidates.
At Wingstop’s King’s Cross location, the business received approximately 800 applications for 50 positions, completing the process from application to onboarding in just five days.
At Parramatta Square, 1,200 applications arrived in ten days.
But perhaps the most interesting aspect of Wingstop’s approach is what happens after a candidate has been hired.
During onboarding, Ranchy asks each new employee for their uniform size and favourite drink.

When they arrive for their first shift, their correctly sized uniform is ready and their preferred drink is waiting. The team then sits down with the new starter over that drink to begin their introduction to the business.
It’s a small gesture, but one that illustrates how automation can support more thoughtful human interactions.
The bigger question for retailers
Wingstop’s experience suggests the opportunity is more nuanced than simply replacing manual recruitment with AI.

The real value lies in identifying where automation can remove delays, reduce inconsistency and improve the experience for candidates, while preserving the human interactions that shape their first impression of an employer.
For retailers, the question may no longer be whether AI belongs in recruitment, but how to ensure the process still feels human.
Watch the full conversation
How did Wingstop implement Ranchy, what has it learned along the way, and what should other retailers consider before introducing AI into their recruitment process?
Watch the on-demand conversation with Jono Spragg and Workday to explore the practical decisions, challenges and lessons behind Wingstop’s approach.

article13.title: Global recommerce giants vying for dominance in Aussie market

hero.headline: Global recommerce giants vying for dominance in Aussie market
hero.subtitle: The rise of tech-savvy recommerce platforms with gamification built in is forcing retailers to redefine resale strategies of their own.
hero.byline: By Nina Hendy, lead journalist, NORA edit
hero.videoAlt: People browsing second-hand clothes at a market stall

sections.content: ustralia has been unable to crack the recommerce market in a substantial way and is now witnessing a new wave of globally dominant players enter the race.
Global recommerce giants Vinted and Whatnot have locked horns on Australian soil, both vying for top spot in the race to win the hearts and open the wallets of local consumers.

Announcing their decision to tackle the Australian market after a number of local platforms have failed to gain traction with consumers over recent years, the duo each believes they have what it takes to muscle in on stalwarts Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and eBay as consumers trade over-consumption for cash.

Research from Afterpay found that the boundaries of commerce are blurring. Consumers, overwhelmed with 'stuff', are looking to the brands that facilitate experiences beyond the point of transaction and are seeking personalised, immersive and intimate moments.

This has led to phenomenal growth forecasts for the recommerce market, which is expected to be worth $US6.75 billion by 2029 in Australia alone as nearly half (46 per cent) of consumers turn to used items each year. The figure, from an Australia Post survey, that reveals that consumers are keen to buy books, music, homewares, collectibles, electronics and fashion second hand, among other items.
Consumer rethink
Consumers have been hungry for new ways to buy and sell their stuff for years, but a number of homegrown recommerce platforms have failed to quell their appetite.

Circonomy focused on repairing, repurposing and reselling dormant or end of use goods, but closed in late 2024, blaming a severe retail downturn and financial unsustainability on its decision to close.
Central rental marketplace ReleaseIt is currently in limbo, with a message on its website promising that it is making site improvements.

Dress hire platform Designerex went into administration last year but since the platform was plucked out of administration by the Sarai family based in Queensland, but it's impossible to know whether it's still a hit with consumers.

Circular economy entrepreneur Yas Grigaliunas also launched Circular Australia three years ago and quickly became a multi-million-dollar player in the recommerce sector but ultimately closed the platform down.

Despite moving onto another successful enterprise in another industry sector, Grigaliunas admits that it takes a lot of investment and time to bring something like Circular Australia together. “It's not just about pushing out a platform. We were really omni-channel, which was a real differentiator in the success that we had.”

She describes it as an unfortunate ending. “My enterprise got to a point where we appointed a CEO, and sadly even with additional capital, we could not recover from decisions that were made at CEO level that didn't support the business.”

Grigaliunas believes that retailers should be considering how to integrate recommerce into their own platforms. “The problem is that I can't walk into a retailer and buy something second-hand, I have to buy it on other platforms like Depop or eBay, which don't give me that brand experience. That's where brands should be trying to cash in.”
Platforms to play

Rival reseller platform Depop has been in the local market since 2019. The platform recently removed the 10% seller fee, charging buyers 5 per cent instead, which is similar to other resale platforms, including Vinted.
The move aligns Depop's fee structure with the UK and US, where removing selling fees saw a 45 per cent increase in listings. In May 2026, Depop received 2.84 million Australian visits.

CEO Peter Semple says: “Every item on our platform starts with someone who chooses to list it, style it, photograph it and ship it. Removing selling fees means more of every sale stays with the people who earned it and we hope it will encourage more people to take their first step into selling second hand.”

In response, eBay has pushed out a new innovation in recent months to bolster engagement and community-driven shopping events, building in live, interactive features such as real-time chat, instant purchasing, rapid-fire auctions and 'popcorn' bidding that extends timers when new bids come in linked to live listings.

With massive reach across Europe, Vinted is confident it can dominate in Australia. It enables sellers to list for free and keep 100 per cent of what they earn, with payment and shipping built into the app. Once the item is purchased, sellers receive a prepaid shipping label to drop off at an Australia Post location. Sellers also keep every dollar they make.

The platform's own research shows nine in 10 Australians have bought or sold second hand, and over half of sellers listed more items in the past year than the year before. The data also shows that 88 per cent of Australians have items at home they could sell, and nearly one in eight believe those items are worth over $1,000.
Unlocking value

Recommerce is growing on the back of a shift on consumer behaviour as they favour buying and selling pre-owned goods to unlock value from items they already own, opting for longevity and sustainability over the latest fad item. Decluttering has also become a way of life amid a cost-of-living crisis.

But this means that retailers are no longer simply competing with each other. Instead, they are up against community-driven marketplaces, someone selling pre-loved items from their own wardrobe, a collector building a following or a creator recommending products to their audience.

Baby Bunting, RM Williams, Patagonia, IKEA, fashion brands Eva's Sunday and Bassike have all explored their own versions of resale, repair or circularity initiatives in response to changing consumer expectations to extend product life.

The Iconic has also used its scale to make circularity convenient and mainstream for its two million active customers, launching circularity hub RE-ICONIC late last year to give members a chance to discover pre-loved fashion, book tailoring and alterations or buy cheaper repaired clothing.

Outdoor brand Kathmandu was ahead of the curve, offering in-store and partner repair services. When products can't be repaired, customers can return used or faulty gear through recycling partners, diverting materials from landfill.
The brand's CEO Megan Welch believes this has reinforced trust in the brand and strengthened its reputation as a responsible outdoor brand focused on longevity rather than replacement.

Recommerce isn't just another marketplace entering Australia. It's a change in how consumers think about ownership as they move between new, pre-owned and reselling items, explains Kirsten Ridgway, Grant Thornton Partner.
The big shift is that consumers are no longer asking ‘Do I want this product? They're also asking, ‘What will it be worth when I'm finished with it?,’ Ridgway says.

However, she describes the rise in recommerce as a slow burn. “While consumer adoption has steadily grown over many years, many retailers have been slower to embrace resale and circular models because the commercial returns aren't always immediate or easy to measure.

“What's changing now is that the scale of consumer demand is becoming too significant to ignore, and retailers are increasingly recognising that resale can strengthen customer loyalty, drive engagement and extend the lifetime of both the customer and the product” Ridgway says.
Retailers contemplating whether to participate in this new ecosystem have been warned to tread carefully given that recommerce introduces operational complexity for retailers.

Ridgway points out that unlike traditional retail, recommerce requires processes for intake, inspection, grading, pricing and presentation, all of which need to be executed consistently to maintain customer trust.
Retailers that succeed at recommerce tend to invest in clear condition standards, transparent product information and strong operational discipline,” Ridgway says.

hero.subtitle: Birdeye’s Tony Van-Eyk on AI visibility, reviews and where retail leaders should start

He covers why reviews rank second in AI visibility, how to decide which jobs belong to AI, and why retail leaders should start with small wins.

hero.headline: Retail at a turning point
hero.subtitle: What the Berlin Retail Congress signals for the industry ahead
hero.byline: By Peter Knock, NORA Berlin correspondent

sections.content: lobal retail leaders meeting in Berlin delivered a message that will resonate strongly in Australia: volatility is here to stay, customers are changing faster, and AI is quickly becoming part of day-to-day retail operations. For local retailers, the challenge is to stay resilient while sharpening value, relevance and productivity.
What Australian retailers should take from Berlin

The clearest takeaway from the World Retail Congress and the Federation of International Retail Associations meeting was that uncertainty is no longer temporary. Cost pressure, subdued spending, supply chain complexity and stronger competition are now built into the retail environment.
For Australian businesses, strategy must focus on resilience, disciplined execution and the ability to adapt quickly as conditions change.
Key insight 01 - Cost pressure and competition

Australian retailers are managing inflationary pressure, freight complexity, energy costs, labour challenges and a more value-conscious consumer. Those pressures are changing assumptions around pricing, investment and expansion. At the same time, competition is coming from every direction, including digital marketplaces and cross-border sellers, making differentiation more important than ever.

The congress also reinforced that retail should be recognised as part of Australia’s economic and social infrastructure. That strengthens the case for practical policy settings on competition, payments, customs, workforce issues and AI governance. For the sector, advocacy is no longer separate from strategy.
Key insight 02 - The customer shift

Customers are no longer moving neatly through a traditional path to purchase. They compare more, switch channels faster and expect stronger value, convenience and relevance. For Australian retailers, that means investing in loyalty, local area marketing, service, fulfilment and connected digital-physical experiences. In slower-growth categories, clear differentiation, whether through private label, service, sustainability or in-store experience, is becoming critical to protecting margin and staying relevant.
Key insight 03 - AI and productivity

AI was one of the strongest themes across the event, but the debate has shifted from experimentation to application. For retailers, the most immediate value is likely to come from pricing, assortment, marketing content, customer service and workforce productivity. The key challenge now is to invest with discipline, supported by stronger data, governance and leadership capability.
For Australian retail, the implication is clear: lift productivity, improve decision-making and adopt AI in ways that strengthen service and trust, not just reduce cost.
Key insight 04 - Berlin retail innovation

Bikini Berlin offered a compelling example of how physical retail can become a platform for innovation, experience and experimentation rather than just transaction. Positioned as a concept shopping mall, it blends architecture, design and curated retail to showcase emerging brands and new ideas in a highly visible consumer setting.

One standout example was SHIFT, a microfactory created by VORN – The Berlin Fashion Hub, which demonstrates how fashion design, digital production and on-demand manufacturing can come together in a live retail environment. The model allows designers and brands to explore more local, agile and sustainable production, while giving shoppers direct exposure to the future of fashion creation. Overall, Bikini Berlin reflects a broader shift in retail towards spaces that combine commerce, storytelling, technology and circular innovation.
Bottom line

The Berlin discussions pointed to a sector that must become more resilient, more customer-centred and more technologically capable at the same time. Retailers that move early on productivity, customer relevance and AI capability will be better placed than those waiting for conditions to stabilise.

This is a moment for deliberate action. The retailers best positioned for the next phase will be those that protect resilience, sharpen their proposition and stay engaged in the policy settings shaping the future of the sector.
Key action points for retailers

items: Strengthen planning for softer demand, cost pressure and global disruption.
Protect cash flow while continuing to invest in priority transformation.
Focus on value, loyalty and distinctive customer experience.
Review supply chain, store and fulfilment models for flexibility and efficiency.
Prioritise AI use cases that improve productivity, service and decision-making.
Invest in the governance and capability needed to scale AI responsibly.
Stay active on policy and industry advocacy.

article16.title: The future of shopping might look a lot like its past

hero.headline: The future of shopping might look a lot like its past
hero.subtitle: As live selling gains momentum in Australia, Whatnot's Alex McCauley believes the next evolution of e-commerce could bring the missing human connection back to retail.

sections.content: Australia’s retailers have spent two decades learning how to sell online.
Now a new generation of platforms is asking them to sell live.

It's a trend that might seem counterintuitive in an increasingly digital world. While online shopping has made buying almost anything easier than ever, conversations, personal connections and a sense of community that once defined the retail experience can sometimes get lost along the way.
Live commerce is attempting to bring those elements back, combining the convenience of e-commerce with the spontaneity and interaction of shopping in person.
And if history is any indication, the retailers who are sceptical today may eventually find themselves playing catch-up.
Speaking at a recent industry gathering in Sydney, Whatnot Australia's general manager Alex McCauley drew parallels between the emergence of live selling and the early days of e-commerce.
Twenty years ago, he observed, many retailers expected a handful of online specialists to dominate digital shopping while traditional businesses continued trading in physical stores.
Some built websites simply to establish an online presence, without necessarily expecting them to become significant sales channels.
But consumer behaviour changed.
As shoppers became increasingly comfortable buying online, having an e-commerce presence moved from an optional extra to an essential part of doing business.
McCauley pointed to earlier assumptions that products such as furniture and cars would never successfully transition to online sales.
Over time, those expectations changed too, as consumers developed trust in digital platforms and younger generations embraced new ways of shopping.
Today, he sees live commerce at a similarly formative stage.
The concept is relatively simple. A seller goes live with a collection of products, introduces each item and invites viewers to participate in real-time bidding.

But unlike traditional e-commerce, where the experience is often solitary and transactional, live selling creates an opportunity for interaction between sellers and buyers, and among shoppers themselves.

sections.alt: Live selling and shopping through Whatnot.

sections.content: “People visit a store for the conversation,” McCauley told attendees.
“Unfortunately the economics of retail have squeezed that conversation thin.”
It's an observation that speaks to a broader tension facing traditional retailers.
As shopping has become increasingly digital, the human interaction that once defined the retail experience has become harder to replicate.
For platforms such as Whatnot, which began with Funko Pops before expanding into trading cards and sports cards, community has been central to the experience.
The platform opened to Australian sellers in October 2024 at a trading card show in Melbourne, initially attracting buyers and sellers united by shared interests.
“There was just this immediate appetite here,” McCauley said, reflecting on the early response from Australian consumers.
While collectables helped establish its audience, categories such as women's fashion are opening up new possibilities for live commerce.
One example McCauley shared involved Australian fashion label Romance Was Born.
During a warehouse sale at Sydney's Paddington Town Hall, a Whatnot employee was determined to demonstrate the potential of live selling.
Having heard that the label's general manager would be arriving to help set up the sale, she waited for an opportunity to pitch the idea.
Eventually, she was given five minutes to make her case.

The label put out its leftover stock, the employee went live with little more than a ring light and an iPhone and, two hours later, the live sale had matched a full day of warehouse sales, with the weakest stock left.
“I think it was better than my team’s plan,” McCauley said.
The anecdote illustrates the potential for live commerce to turn what might otherwise be a conventional retail transaction into something more immediate and engaging.
For retailers, it also speaks to what happens when the shopping experience becomes as important as the product itself.
McCauley's perspective on changing industries has been shaped by an unconventional career.

Before leading Whatnot's Australian operations, he worked in law, served as an Australian diplomat in Tel Aviv and helped establish the Tech Council of Australia, which launched in 2021 with 25 member companies.
His experience persuading businesses to embrace a collective vision offers an interesting parallel to the challenge facing emerging retail platforms today.
Introducing a new way of doing business requires more than technology. It demands trust, relationships and a willingness to challenge established thinking.
And while the technology behind live commerce may be new to many Australian retailers, the underlying appeal is anything but.

For generations, shopping was as much a social experience as a commercial one. From market stalls to neighbourhood boutiques, the exchange between seller and customer was often part of what made the experience memorable.
Live selling offers a digital interpretation of that familiar dynamic.
It also challenges the assumption that progress in retail must always mean greater automation, fewer interactions and increasingly frictionless transactions.
Perhaps the next evolution of e-commerce won't be about removing people from the shopping experience, but finding new ways to bring them together.
For businesses curious about live selling but uncertain about where to begin, McCauley's advice at the gathering was simple.
“Forget about making it perfect.”
It's a sentiment that captures a lesson from the history of retail innovation.
New ways of doing business rarely arrive fully formed, and the businesses willing to experiment are often the first to understand their potential.
After all, the future of shopping may not be decided by the retailers who perfect the technology, but by the customers who decide how they want to use it.
And increasingly, those customers may be looking for something that shopping has always offered at its best, a conversation.

hero.headline: The great retail decoupling
hero.subtitle: The Australian consumer is in better shape than the mood in most boardrooms suggests, but the gap between retail winners and losers is set to widen.

sections.content: he Australian consumer is in better shape than the mood in most boardrooms suggests; ABS household spending accelerated to c7% year-on-year in July, its strongest pace in over a year, confidence is back to pre-Middle East conflict levels and household deposits are fast approaching $1.8 trillion.
The consumer can and will spend, the question is are retailers giving them a reason to?
This was a key theme through the recent retailer results, whereby the gap between winners and losers grew and those companies that had the right product at the right price and the right time won.

We are seeing this across a raft of categories: In grocery Woolworths Ooshies promotion was a resounding success, with the group recording a 7.6% lift in sales for the first 8wks of FY27, as consumers (or the parents of) responded to a unique, differentiated limited time offer.

In online Amazon continued to positively surprise and delight, further strengthening its delivery promise in August driving both increased order frequency but more significantly lifting customer expectations. We are seeing incumbents respond with the likes of Coles, Woolworths and Super Retail Group accelerating roll-out plans to leverage their competitive advantage and strengthen ultra-fast delivery and click & collect.
Across non-food we saw brands with unique offers targeting specific consumer sub-sets deliver strong results with Universal Stores, Skin Candy and Lovisa all performing well.

Health remains a key growth channel; with GLP-1 sales were up >50% y/y driving strong growth for both Priceline and Chemist Warehouse, while also having positive flow on effects across categories such as vitamins and high-protein products in grocery. On the flip-side, it is having a negative effect on areas such as snacking and liquor, but this also presents opportunities via smaller (often higher margin) pack sizes.

There were some weaker results, with the impact of growing competition, consumers deferring purchases until key sales events and AI prevalent in areas such as electronics, local marketplaces and department stores.

Looking forward there are five themes we are watching into FY27; First, the “macro versus micro” decoupling — strong aggregate spending data continues to suggest the consumer is in a better place than company updates would suggest. We expect FY27 to be a year where companies that get the small things right via product, price and service win – we expect the gap between winners and losers to widen. Second, margin; pressure from freight, the 4.75% minimum wage increase and rising promotional I creates risk around profit margins into FY27. Third, a capex tug-of-war between store expansion and supply chain, where we think the latter matters more given marketplace growth in Australia, and specifically Amazon which we expect to surpass $10b of GMV this year. Fourth, the monetisation of adjacencies — A real opportunity exists for brands to better monetise traffic via partnerships, media and loyalty; Woolworths is best practice locally, with this channel totaling >$300m of profit (EBIT) in FY26. Fifth, AI, the productivity and revenue opportunity are understand, Agentic is the key theme for 2027, it will democratize the store front and brands need to understand how to embrace this.

So how should companies position over the next twelve months? Ignore the temptation to make a macro call and ask three questions: What is your competitive moat? How do you leverage this to grow share of wallet? What productivity / adjacency opportunities exist to lift ROIC? For retailers, that means leaning into, and widening, your moat rather than chasing the cycle — winning on the full value equation of range, price, service and quality, not price alone; building genuine product differentiation rather than renting someone else’s; and monetising data, media and marketplace adjacencies before a competitor — or Amazon — does it for you.

We remain optimistic on the outlook, but expect the market to bifurcate with brands ability to segment and target the customer and grow share of wallet key. The gap between winners and losers will widen.

article18.title: The state of AI in retail

hero.headline: The state of AI in retail
hero.subtitle: Australian retail is racing towards AI. But how embedded is it really?

sections.content: AI has quickly moved from experimentation to a strategic priority for Australian retailers. Yet while investment, pilots and ambition are accelerating, the way businesses are approaching AI varies significantly.
NORA and Shopify surveyed 184 retail executives representing 127 companies across Australia to understand what AI adoption actually looks like on the ground.

The research explores adoption maturity, ownership, internal capability, budgets and implementation approaches, creating a benchmark for an industry moving quickly while navigating many of the same challenges.
The numbers tell an interesting story.
82% of retail leaders surveyed have agentic commerce modernisation on their roadmap.
Yet just 8% believe AI is fully embedded in how their organisation operates.
That gap between ambition and operational maturity is where many of the industry's biggest questions now sit.
Why measure AI adoption now?
Over the past 18 months, NORA has brought retail leaders together through multiple Retail GenAI Summits to discuss how AI is changing their businesses.
One thing has become increasingly clear: there is no single playbook.
Retailers are moving at different speeds, placing ownership in different parts of the business and taking very different approaches to capability, investment and implementation.
The State of AI in Retail was created to establish a shared baseline: what retailers are doing today, what they believe is working, where investment is heading and what is getting in the way.
Fielded ahead of NORA's Retail GenAI Summit in September 2026, the research provides a snapshot of the AI-engaged end of the Australian retail market at a pivotal point in its adoption.
184 retail leaders. 127 companies. One view of where Australian retail really sits on AI.

article19.title: The performance trap: what an uneven marketing split costs Australian retailers

hero.headline: The performance trap: what an uneven marketing split costs Australian retailers
hero.subtitle: Australian retailers may be spending more to win customers while underinvesting in the brand that keeps them. At NORA’s Hyperelevance Summit, presenters argued that brand building and a genuine sense of purpose can lift loyalty and margin together.

sections.content: Most Australian businesses have developed an expensive habit.
According to NORA’s Hyperelevance Summit, they put 90 percent of their budgets into performance marketing. Brand building gets the remaining 10 percent.
Price competition may explain why.

Will On, co-founder of Shippit, said pricing pressure is one big lever for the retailers he works with. When The Iconic launched free delivery, he said, it “changed the game for everyone,” and rivals had to match it. “When rivals keep matching each other’s offers, the spend that wins the next sale can look like the safest bet.”

Performance marketing mostly reaches the 5 percent of buyers who are buying now. The other 95 percent are in consideration or will buy soon, and brand investment builds that future demand today. Tomorrow’s growth comes at lower cost from a much larger pool of customers.
Best practice sits at 60 percent brand building and 40 percent performance marketing, according to Binet & Field’s analysis of more than 1,000 commercial cases.

The first cost is margin. Presenters put the rise in performance marketing costs at 60 percent over the last four years. Customer acquisition costs rise with it, and customers switch brands for a 5 percent discount, which shows how little brand loyalty remains.
Speakers called the point where rising costs meet thin loyalty the ‘performance wall’.
Jordana Macfarlaine, formerly of Havaianas Australia, described the same pressure.
Rising acquisition costs are “really hard for a business to continue to keep up with,” she said, and “just churning out digital paid ads is not having any human connection or emotion in any way.”

She gave the brand-side explanation for why customers leave. Without consistent storytelling, she said, “you are not relevant. And people will move on to the next product, the next brand, because they’re not really loyal to you.”
The second cost is control. A defensible brand, speakers said, protects retailers from global marketplaces such as Temu and Shein.
The third is pricing power. Reduced price sensitivity is among the most underrated commercial benefits of emotional brand building.
Kieron Ritchard, former CEO of Fantastic Furniture, put the point plainly on the opening panel.
“Brands drive premium,” he said. “A brand earns that premium by truly understanding its foundations.”
Understanding those foundations starts inside the business.
Purpose, Ritchard said, “connects first with your employee proposition, and then in turn to your customer value proposition.”
That sequence is how purpose builds brand equity. Customers who connect with what a retailer stands for have a reason to keep choosing it when a rival offers a discount.
Impact storytelling is the strongest way to build that connection.

Giving back taps into hope, empathy and community. It gives customers something bigger to belong to, beyond the reach of any rival’s discount or ad spend. It builds warmth, trust and lasting affinity among customers who will buy later.
“The commitment has to last and match what the brand cares about because customers can read a mismatch as inauthentic,” Ritchard said.

In Australia, 74 percent of consumers seek out purpose-driven retailers, according to the summit and yet only 12 percent of Australian brands currently communicate a unified emotional brand story. That gap is unbuilt brand equity.
According to Macfarlaine, building that equity takes patience.
The former Marketing Director of Havaianas Australia said it took Havaianas “probably a year” before it started brand partnerships, because the team “needed to build that brand almost again.”
Every retailer decides how much more to pay for customers who leave for a 5 percent discount. Brand equity decides how many of them stay.

hero.headline: Bridging worlds to thrive
hero.subtitle: "Purpose can no longer be peripheral it must become essential."
hero.byline: By Jeremy Meltzer, founder & CEO, i=Change

sections.content: or decades, business has operated under a singular mandate - maximize short-term shareholder value at all costs. Social and environmental consequences are someone else’s problem.
This version of business began as an idea, which enough of us accepted until it was considered normal.
Yet ‘normal’ has come with enormous cost.
This opens the tantalising opportunity for a new idea, a new normal that updates how we do business - and why.

As retail falters, a new idea is already emerging that could make retail ‘hyper relevant’ and achieve the growth it seeks, but it must reflect the need of our time. It must reflect what we as individuals - and consumers - increasingly care about; living in healthy communities in reciprocity with a thriving natural environment that sustains life for all.
Yet to achieve this - to put it simply - we must grow up.
For what is shiny cannot fill the hole. It never could and never will.

Yet while the archetypal yearning to contribute to something bigger than ourselves is alive in us, it seems only few business leaders understand the power of engaging customers with head and heart. When integrated with authenticity and transparency, their businesses thrive.

If retail is ‘just’ a transaction at an agreed value exchange; I receive a shirt, you receive money, and not much else matters, it seems inevitable we would arrive at this point in our timeline. For just across the horizon, our current model of consumption, reliant upon manufactured desires is becoming irrelevant.

We know this in our hearts, but if our heads need validation, it’s in rising costs per acquisition, consumer burnout and sales overwhelm. Alongside anxiety-causing awareness of environmental challenges, we’re starting to check out - and not in the way retailers would like.

I remember my grandparents came from Europe with hand-cut suits and tailored dresses. Shopping was not a casual activity. It was an indulgence once a year. Money was spent on dinners with friends, travel, experiences, and saving for the grandchildren.
So how did we get from there to here?

Edward Bernays - credited as the grandfather of PR - worked from 1910 to the 1960s to shift advertising from functional need to unconscious emotional desire. Using ideas from his uncle, Sigmund Freud, he targeted irrational impulses, fear, and status.

Bernays realised it could be simple to link products to social identity. He famously framed women smoking cigarettes as ‘torches of freedom’, as a way to reclaim their power. By manipulating cultural norms and subconscious desires, products became symbols of personal expression. He effectively created modern consumerism, where buying became an act of self-fulfillment rather than practical necessity.
I doubt Bernays imagined the disparities of wealth and status his work would create. I wonder if he would regret its consequences, and impact on people and planet?
So here we are.

It seems clear that ‘purpose’ can no longer be peripheral, but must become essential. Consumers are responding powerfully to brands that make their purchases meaningful, with authentic storytelling that engages heads and hearts.

So as business leaders we have a choice. Like a slowly sinking ship, we can hold on to the same ideas - or we can be courageous, unleash the heroic spirit of business and in doing so, also unlock the growth we seek.

Today, customers expect the brands to have ‘skin in the game’, to be transparently giving to people and planet. Whether that’s empowering women and girls, tackling climate change, or supporting local communities - purpose and profit have become mutually reinforcing drivers of business performance. It also builds visceral loyalty that traditional marketing cannot buy.
The businesses that thrive understand the power of this brand equity - they’re building for legacy not only short-term sales. They’re part of the solution.
I wonder what my grandparents would say, sitting in their tailored clothes next to their grandchildren dressed in the latest fashion?

Let us not forget we are humans selling to humans, and we have been gathering around fires telling stories forever. Stories inspire us to action. We have an opportunity as an industry to tell a bigger story - and one that also builds a bigger business.

Yet it starts with us. Australian retail can emerge as a global leader of purpose-driven business. We can ‘be the change’ we seek, steward thriving businesses that address the needs of the time, and build legacy brands of which we can be proud.
